pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic — Ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), REPRESENTATIONAL. Represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, and mental images — the bridge between the concepts (combining / taking away) and their symbolic notation. Children externalise a calculation so they can reason about and communicate it.
• Standards — UK (DfE NC Mathematics, Y1): solve problems 'using concrete objects and pictorial representations'; the concrete–pictorial–abstract progression is the backbone of KS1 additive work.
• Standards — US (CCSS-M): K.OA.1 'represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings…, acting out situations, verbal explanations, expressions, or equations'.
• Operational details — Deliberately cycle the SAME calculation through multiple representations — real objects → drawing → finger/mental image → spoken → number sentence — and ask the child to connect them ('show me where the 2 is in your drawing'). The aim is fluency in MOVING between representations, and progressively internalising them as mental images so counting-all can give way to more efficient strategies.
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 4): use cubes/counters to show a given addition or subtraction. Tier B (age 5): draw a picture that matches a spoken add/subtract situation. Tier C (age 5-6): represent the same problem two ways (e.g. objects AND a drawing) and explain how they show the same calculation.
bestPractices: Cycle ONE calculation through several representations and explicitly link them ('point to the 3 in the cubes, now in your drawing') — the skill is the mapping between representations, not any single one.
Move along concrete → pictorial → mental image → symbolic, encouraging children to eventually 'see it in their head' so representations become efficient mental tools rather than crutches.
Use consistent structured models (ten-frames, part-whole, fingers) so representations accumulate meaning rather than being ad hoc each time.
Have children narrate their representation aloud ('I drew 5 and crossed out 2') to tie drawing to action to language.
Value the child's own drawings/jottings while nudging toward clearer, more mathematical ones (dots/marks over detailed pictures) to keep focus on quantity.
keyRepresentations: Ten-frames and five-frames as structured object layouts
Children's own drawings/jottings (dots, marks, crossing-out for removal)
Mental images and the spoken number sentence as the bridge to symbols
commonMisconceptions: Treating each representation as a separate, unrelated task and not seeing that the objects, drawing and number sentence all show the SAME calculation.
Drawing elaborate pictures that obscure quantity (detailed apples instead of countable dots), losing the mathematical point.
Staying dependent on concrete objects and not progressing toward drawings/mental images, so efficiency never develops.
Mis-mapping between representations — e.g. drawing the total when the story described only one part.
Using a drawing as decoration after getting an answer another way, rather than as a tool to find or explain the answer.

learn.summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), help children represent addition and subtraction using objects, drawings, fingers, mental images, spoken language, and number sentences — and, crucially, move fluidly between these so they see that they all show the SAME calculation. Deliberately cycle one calculation through multiple representations and link them explicitly ('show me where the 2 is in your drawing'), progressing from concrete toward mental imagery so efficient strategies can replace counting-all.

activities.title: Linked windows onto one calculation
feedback: When the linked panes update together, say: 'The two counters, the two dots, and the 2 in your sentence all show the same two — they match.'
If the child predicts the hidden drawing correctly, affirm: 'You pictured it in your head before you saw it — that's carrying the maths in your mind.'
If the child can't find the matching two in another pane, prompt: 'You tapped the 2 — point to where the two counters are, and the two dots.'
activities.rationale: This topic is about fluidly moving between representations. A live linked canvas where acting in one pane updates the others, with a tap-to-highlight tool that glows the same quantity across all panes, makes the 'these all show the same thing' insight visible and manipulable. The hide-a-pane challenge pushes toward mental imagery, the developmental goal. The linked updating and highlight are optional illustrative mechanisms, not mandatory; a fixed worked example with tappable cross-links can anchor the same idea.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve addition and subtraction problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations (concrete-pictorial-abstract progression).
K.OA.1: represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, acting out, verbal explanations, expressions or equations.
Explicitly linking multiple representations of the same calculation and progressing toward mental imagery supports additive reasoning.
learnerActions: Place counters onto a mat to show a given sum such as 3 + 2.
Watch linked representations update together: a ten-frame fills, a dot-drawing sketches itself, and the number sentence 3 + 2 = 5 assembles alongside the counters.
Tap the '2' in the number sentence and see exactly two counters, two dots, and two ten-frame cells light up at once across every pane.
Try a 'cover a window' challenge: predict what the drawing will look like before it is revealed, then check.
activities.intendedInsight: The objects, drawing, ten-frame and number sentence are not separate exercises — they are the same quantity shown different ways; and I can begin to carry the picture in my head.

activities.title: Show it with cubes, then with a drawing
feedback: If the child draws elaborate apples, gently redirect: 'Try quick dots so we can count them fast — the number is what matters.'
When drawing and cubes match, say: 'You showed 3 + 2 with cubes AND with dots — both tell the same story.'
If the child narrates the action while drawing, affirm the link between drawing, action, and words.
activities.rationale: Having children produce their own representations and map between them (the two-ways-and-explain checkpoint) builds the generative skill, not just recognition. Narrating aloud ties drawing to action to language; nudging toward dots over detailed pictures keeps focus on quantity.
sourceClaims: Y1 pupils solve addition and subtraction problems using concrete objects and pictorial representations (concrete-pictorial-abstract progression).
Explicitly linking multiple representations of the same calculation and progressing toward mental imagery supports additive reasoning.
learnerActions: Use cubes or counters to show a spoken addition, e.g. build 3 and 2 pushed together to make 5.
Draw a picture (dots or marks) that matches the same calculation.
Narrate aloud what you did, e.g. 'I drew 3 dots and 2 more dots, and that makes 5.'
Point to the '3' and the '2' in the cubes, then point to them in your drawing.
activities.intendedInsight: I can represent the same calculation two different ways and show how they correspond, using quick countable marks rather than detailed pictures.

activities.title: Enact subtraction as taking away
feedback: If the child builds a pile of 5 and a pile of 1 for 5 − 1, re-link the minus to the action: 'Start with 5, now take 1 away — how many are left?'
If the structure is right but the count slips (e.g. says 5 − 1 = 3), scaffold a careful one-to-one recount; the subtraction idea is intact, so don't reteach it.
When removal is enacted correctly, affirm: 'You started with five and took one away — that's what the minus means here.'
activities.rationale: A common error is treating any two numbers as 'put together', building 5 and 1 as separate piles for 5 − 1. Enacting the removal and attaching the number sentence links the minus symbol to the take-away action. Translating BOTH ways — reading a model as a sentence and enacting a sentence with objects — is what demonstrates a secure representation-operation link.
sourceClaims: K.OA.1: represent addition and subtraction with objects, fingers, mental images, drawings, acting out, verbal explanations, expressions or equations.
Explicitly linking multiple representations of the same calculation and progressing toward mental imagery supports additive reasoning.
learnerActions: Start with 5 cubes and show 5 − 1 by actually removing one cube, leaving four.
Say the number sentence aloud: '5 take away 1 leaves 4, so 5 − 1 = 4.'
Explain which cube you took away and how many are left.
Contrast this with 4 + 1: show how combining to make 5 is different from taking away to leave 4.
activities.intendedInsight: One way subtraction works is taking away: starting with an amount and removing part of it. That is different from putting two groups together.

activities.title: Match and talk about representations (supporting activities)
feedback: After a correct match, ask the child to point to the matching part in each ('where is the 2 in both?') so matching becomes connecting.
For 'another way', if the child restates the same drawing, prompt a different format: 'Could you show it on a ten-frame instead?'
activities.rationale: Matching (drawing ↔ number sentence) checks that a child recognises correspondence and can sit within broader early-number practice, but a scored linear matching task does not by itself develop the generative move-between-representations skill and is developmentally light at 4-6; use it as support, not the main vehicle. 'Show me another way' dialogue can prompt re-representation, but the drawing/object work is the manual/visual part, so pair the talk with a drawing or object tool rather than relying on talk alone.
learnerActions: Match a drawing to the number sentence that shows the same calculation.
Respond to the prompt 'Show me another way to draw that' and produce a second representation.
Use structured models consistently — ten-frames, five-frames, or a part-part-whole ('cherry') diagram — so representations accumulate meaning.
activities.intendedInsight: The same calculation can be recognised across formats, and structured models give it a consistent, reusable shape.

constraints: The core skill is MAPPING between representations, not mastering any single one — always link them explicitly ('point to the 3 in the cubes, now in your drawing').

Matching or recognition-style tasks assess recognition of correspondence but do not elicit the independent construction of a child's own representations; keep them as a supporting check, not the main activity.

Dialogue prompts ('show me another way') work best alongside a drawing or object tool, since much of the re-representation work here is manual/visual; talk can still prompt and explain re-representation.
Tap-to-highlight, live-updating linked panes, and the hide-a-pane challenge are optional illustrative mechanisms to make the correspondence concrete — not mandatory features.
Value children's own jottings while nudging toward quick countable marks (dots) over elaborate pictures, so quantity stays in focus.
Aim to progress concrete → pictorial → mental image → symbolic so representations become efficient mental tools rather than permanent crutches; do not leave children dependent on objects.

Paper/cubes and an on-screen canvas offer different experiences; neither is required, and a fixed worked example can still anchor the parallel-representations idea even though it cannot be manipulated.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

The row claimed the linked live canvas shows the insight 'in a way no static medium can' and that 3D 'adds nothing'; these comparative-necessity claims are not established by the cited sources and have been softened to scoped affordances/limits.

Arithmetic in examples was checked: 3 + 2 = 5, 5 − 1 = 4, 4 + 1 = 5 are correct. The row's own distractor '3 + 2 = 6' (and the analogous '5 − 1 = 3') are deliberate error examples for the miscount pattern and appear only in a feedback/diagnostic context, never presented as correct.
Two source claims (CCSS K.OA.1 and the NCETM/Bruner CPA claim) are marked verified:false in the row; treat their evidential strength as unconfirmed.

probeDeeper: Point to the part of the cubes that is the '3', and the part that is the '2'.
Now show me the same thing with a drawing instead of cubes.
For 5 − 1, which cube did you take away, and how many are left?
Could you show 4 + 1 with the cubes so it makes 5 too?
assess.correctAnswer: Reads the cubes as 3 + 2 = 5 (combining); then models 5 − 1 by starting with five cubes and taking one away, leaving four, and can say 5 − 1 = 4.

errorPatterns.pattern: For 5 − 1 builds two groups (5 and 1) and combines them — treats any two numbers as 'put together', not enacting removal.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Re-link the minus symbol to the take-away action on the cubes; narrate 'start with 5, take 1 away, how many left'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child makes a pile of 5 and a pile of 1 for 5 − 1 rather than removing one from five.

errorPatterns.pattern: Represents only the numbers, not the operation — lays out 3 and 2 but cannot say the model means 3 + 2 = 5.
errorPatterns.nextMove: Model the joining action and attach the sentence; move deliberately between story → cubes → number sentence.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Child describes the cubes as '3 and 2' with no combining or total.

errorPatterns.pattern: Correct representation but miscounts when reading it off (says 3 + 2 = 6).
errorPatterns.nextMove: Scaffold a one-to-one recount; the representation concept is intact, so do not reteach it.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Structure is right, but the count of the combined cubes slips.

responseLevels.gap: Cannot translate a model into a sentence, or builds an addition when asked to show a subtraction.
responseLevels.full: Moves fluently both ways — interprets a concrete model as a sentence and enacts a sentence with objects — including distinguishing take-away from combining.
responseLevels.partial: Translates in one direction only (reads a model OR builds from a sentence), or needs support to connect the operation to the action.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are 3 cubes and 2 more cubes pushed together (show them). What number sentence does this show? Now YOU show me 5 − 1 using the cubes.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Translating BOTH ways is the test: interpreting a given concrete model into a symbolic sentence, then enacting a symbolic sentence with objects. A child who can only go one way, or who builds '5' and '1' as two separate piles for 5 − 1 (treating − as +), reveals a shaky link between representation and operation.
